newsitem.title: CANADA: The Internet and your toaster.
newsitem.headline: The Internet and your toaster.

text.p: TORONTO, Reuter - It was only a few years ago when arrival of a new computer to your office or home could induce rapturous joy and a renewed sense of optimism.
There was so much promise in the blinking lights and authoritative sounding hard drive each time you powered up the machine set up in a hallowed spot in the den or office cubicle.
Somehow you just knew that machine could solve problems, introduce time saving techniques, and, well, do everything but make coffee.
But somewhere along the line computers became commodities, something that could be turned out in Taiwan and Texas and not exclusively -- it at all -- in Silicon Valley.
While computers perform many wonderful tasks, the PC for many has become little more than a glorified typewriter or a personal arcade centre, sans the tokens.

The Internet has revitalised many of those PCs and probably helped boost sales for a time. But some have wondered if the PC's reign will soon be eclipsed with the rise of more intelligent devices requiring a lot less infernal tinkering.
The future probably rests in the building of more intelligent computing devices that could be easily interconnected with other such devices, more than likely over the Internet.
"Computing is not about computers any more. It is about living," wrote networking guro Nicholas Negroponte, in his book "Being Digital."

The idea is that computers should shrink from display and really become hidden in all kinds of much easier to use devices to make our lives better. We should no longer have to care about how a device carries out a task, just that it does.

David Kline, co-author of "Road Warriors: Dreams and Nightmares Along the Information Highway," argued in a recent Wired Magazine article that life will be indeed be much simpler with these so-called "embedded computers," or tiny crash proof computers on a chip that would be hidden in a variety of consumer items.
This has been happening for some time in the automotive industry which has been steadily tucking away micropocessors to run everything from the brakes to the stereo system.
In an e-mail correspondence, Kline said penetration of PCs into the home was slowing because it was near saturation of households with the income and technology skills to run them.
More than a third of North American homes have PCs but any new sales were now really going towards replacing older models already in place.

Kline said it was not a coincidence that penetration levels were much higher for inexpensive "push button" type devices such as television and telephones -- in more than 90 percent of homes -- and even video game machines -- in 45 percent of homes.

"Clearly, new types of true, consumer-oriented devices are needed to push beyond the current demographic limits and really reach into the broader mass market," San Francisco-based Kline said in the correspondence.

First out of the shoot should be Net-ready televisions that would allow quick access to the Net. One could imagine the possibilities: a dedicated couch potato would surf the broadcast channels and, if still not satisfied, whip over to the Web to try out an Interactive sports page or some all news Web site.

Rather than tinkering with reluctant hard drives or cranky modems, the Web would be a click away on the hand held remote control. Presumably the small computer on a chip in the television would not suffer boggy software browsers or any other of the troubles faced by ever patient Web heads.

So what would be next? How about wired toasters, dishwashers and microwaves that can check into the Net at certain times to fetch operating software or warranty updates while you were sleeping. Or perhaps your compact disk player would rush out each month and download some of the latest hits for a small fee from a music store site.
Clearly, it will soon be time to drop the brawny desk boat anchors for some units with a few more brains.
